Simulation results show improved recovery of structural boundaries and fine details, with the mean peak signal-to-noise ratio increasing from 11.4239 to 22.1719 dB. These findings highlight the potential of diffusion models to make more effective use of limited muon data and broaden the application of accelerator-based muon imaging across scientific and industrial settings.

papers.title: Anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test by $e$-spacings
papers.summary: To perform an anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test, we propose spacing-based \(e\)-processes that control the type-I error rate under arbitrary stopping rules. Based on the maximum spacing of order statistics, we construct spacing-based \(e\)-processes for nonparametrically testing distribution. The resulting procedures are simple and computationally efficient, and are power-consistent. We call them $e$-spacing tests. This approach is especially powerful in detecting localized discrepancy between the data-generating density and the null density. Under mild conditions, the logarithm of the proposed \(e\)-process is asymptotically equivalent to that of the oracle-optimal \(e\)-process. We further generalize the construction from maximal spacing to maximum spacing set in the form of the \(1/k\) fraction of the largest \(m\)th order spacings, as a measure of the lower-level set of density. It boosts power under more global discrepancy from the null. Furthermore, we propose a greedy predictable scheme, via argmax or softmax rules, to combine multiple $e$-spacing testing strategies. We prove that it optimally tunes the $e$-spacing test. The proposed approach is readily generalizable to multivariate testing via a coordinate-wise Rosenblatt-transform. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably relative to the considered anytime-valid competitors as well as various types of multiple test-adjusted Kolmogorov--Smirnov tests.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
papers.summary: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.
papers.comment: 57 pages, 17 figures, 7 tables. In the title, n-DAS denotes an optimizer of order n restricted to the dominant aligned subspace (DAS): 1-DAS for first-order and 2-DAS for second-order methods

papers.title: Approximating Anisotropic Solar Radiation Pressure
papers.summary: Solar radiation pressure (SRP) significantly influences satellite dynamics in high-altitude orbits, depending not only on the satellite's trajectory and attitude but also on its surface optical characteristics. Metallic surfaces, such as solar cells with periodic metal bars, exhibit anisotropic reflection that produces an anisotropic SRP. The difficulty in dealing with anisotropic SRP arises because anisotropic SRP does not have a general analytical solution, and accurate computation therefore requires numerical integration. An analytical formulation of anisotropic SRP is useful for stability analysis and controller design for satellites that exploit SRP. To this end, this paper derives an analytical approximation method to calculate the anisotropic SRP modeled with the Ashikhmin-Shirley model. The anisotropy is approximated using multiple spherical Gaussians. Because the product of spherical Gaussians is also a spherical Gaussian, anisotropic reflection can be expressed in an analytically tractable form. The approximation accuracy of the anisotropic SRP is numerically verified for two cases: weak anisotropy and strong anisotropy.
papers.comment: 33 pages, 21 figures, 4 tables. Accepted manuscript of the article published in Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics

papers.title: Mitigating the Grid Impact of Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers via High-Fidelity Model Flexibility
papers.summary: Gigawatt-scale artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) are being connected at a single point of interconnection (POI) faster than transmission can be reinforced, yet studies of their flexibility rely on DC power flow and simplified load envelopes that omit voltage, cooling dynamics, and workload deadlines. This paper addresses this gap by embedding a high-fidelity AIDC model, with separate inference and training pools, hall thermal mass, PV, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with reactive capability, and a STATCOM, in a five-minute multi-period AC optimal power flow. Simulations on the RTS-GMLC test system show that active-power flexibility mitigates local price spikes and relieves congestion, whereas reactive support from the BESS inverter or a STATCOM is needed to keep the POI voltage away from sagging around its 0.95~pu limit. Sensitivity analyses show that cost-driven charging of large batteries can induce new morning congestion and that storage largely substitutes for wider workload deferral.

papers.title: DetectViT: Test-time Backdoor Detection for Vision Transformers via Inter-Head Attention Discrepancy
papers.summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) now underpin the visual encoders of most multimodal models, but this success comes at a cost: relying on third-party pretrained checkpoints leaves these systems open to backdoor attacks. Existing test-time detection methods rely on either the predicted label or intermediate embeddings, limiting their applicability across diverse tasks and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we study how backdoor triggers affect the multi-head attention mechanism of ViTs and identify two distinct anomalous patterns: $\textit{complete attention hijacking}$, causing the attention to exhibit abnormally high inter-head spatial overlap, and $\textit{partial attention hijacking}$, causing an abnormally large variance in the concentration of the attention distribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose $\textbf{DetectViT}$, a test-time backdoor detection method that requires neither training data, model outputs, nor any prior knowledge of the trigger. DetectViT quantifies the two hijacking phenomena via an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score, with thresholds estimated from a small out-of-distribution (OOD) calibration set drawn from an arbitrary source. Across four representative attacks, diverse architectures (DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA), and downstream tasks (image classification and captioning), DetectViT substantially outperforms all baselines with as few as 64--128 OOD calibration samples, achieving a true positive rate of $100\%$ and a false positive rate of $0.17\%$ on BadCLIP. Notably, it introduces negligible additional overhead by relying solely on attention weights already computed during inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/siquanhuang/DetectViT.

papers.title: Beyond Intelligibility: Fine-Grained Perceptual Assessment of Dysarthric Speech with Auditory Large Language Models
papers.summary: Accurate assessment of dysarthric speech is vital for clinical diagnosis and rehabilitation, yet existing automated methods rely heavily on isolated, single-task models or generic speech quality metrics that fail to disentangle heterogeneous neuromotor deficits. This work presents the first systematic investigation into adapting auditory large language models (ALLMs) for multi-dimensional dysarthric speech assessment under a unified, prompt-conditioned framework. Four representative ALLMs are benchmarked across five clinical perceptual dimensions from the Speech Accessibility Project (SAP): naturalness, monopitch, intelligibility, imprecise consonants, and inappropriate silences. To bridge generic perceptual quality and clinical evaluation, a two-stage training paradigm is explored, leveraging out-of-domain pre-training followed by in-domain clinical adaptation. Experimental results demonstrate that leading ALLMs reliably capture fine-grained pathological variations, exhibiting distinct and complementary strengths across prosodic and articulatory attributes. These findings establish ALLMs as a scalable foundation for clinical speech evaluation and provide practical insights into model selection and multi-task transfer potential.
papers.comment: 5 pages; Haotian Wei, Can Long, and Wen Xian Jim contributed equally

papers.title: A Lower Bound for the Chromatic Number of Ball-Packing Graphs
papers.summary: For every odd prime power $q$, we construct a finite packing of congruent balls in dimension $d=q^2-q+1$ whose contact graph requires at least $2d$ colors. Consequently, the ball-packing chromatic number satisfies $\chiball(q^2-q+1)\ge2(q^2-q+1)$, and the same lower bound holds for congruent-ball packings. The construction starts from the complements of Hubaut's $C_{20}$ graphs and uses their Taylor extensions. We give an explicit finite-field adjacency rule for the $q^3$-vertex graph $H_q$, prove its strong regularity, determine its spectrum and projection matrix, establish $α(H_q)=q$, and construct a two-distance embedding in $\R^{q(q-1)}$. Its Taylor extension $T_q$ has $2(q^3+1)$ vertices. We prove its distance-regularity, compute its intersection array, construct a three-distance embedding in $\R^{d}$, and prove $α(T_q)=q+1$. The chromatic lower bound follows by realizing $T_q$ as the contact graph of equal-radius balls and bounding the size of every color class. All coordinates, distances, and independence bounds are derived explicitly. The case $q=3$ uses the Schläfli and Gosset graphs and gives a packing of 56 congruent balls in $\R^7$ requiring at least 14 colors.

papers.title: Authenticating IoT Data on Ethereum after Pectra and Fusaka: A Cost Study of Signature Schemes, Batching and Anchoring for Agricultural Supply Chain Finance
papers.summary: Blockchain-based supply chain finance can turn the sensor-recorded production history of smallholder farms into verifiable credit evidence, but only if every record is authenticated and anchored at a cost that scales to large device fleets. Ethereum's 2025 Pectra and Fusaka upgrades changed this cost landscape: they added precompiles for BLS12-381 and P-256, repriced calldata and MODEXP, and capped transaction gas at $2^{24}$. We organize the authentication and anchoring of IoT records into three trust levels, from posting a Merkle root through a trusted aggregator to verifying every device signature on-chain, and implement four replay-protected signature designs: ECDSA over secp256k1 and P-256, BLS aggregate signatures with on-chain hash-to-curve, and a pseudonymous identity-based signature with batch verification. Measured as signed transactions under the rules before and after both upgrades, the upgrades mainly changed which designs are feasible, not their cost. Batching and Merkle anchoring cut the cost of ECDSA authentication sixfold, to 8,963 gas per record, and secp256k1 ECDSA remains the cheapest authenticated design: P-256 costs 1.6 times as much, the identity-based design 2.7 times and BLS aggregation 3.9 times, dominated by on-chain hashing to the curve. One transaction carries at most 1,754 ECDSA-authenticated records but only 411 BLS-aggregated ones. On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, pairing-based signing takes 5.7 ms against 0.29 ms for ECDSA. Pairing-based designs pay off only when the application needs their additional properties, and the identity-based design adds key escrow at the key generation centre. The benchmark harness is released for reproducibility.
papers.comment: 22 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24328819

papers.title: Geiss-Besov Regularity of Exit Times of Diffusion Processes
papers.summary: We prove that the truncated exit times of possibly degenerate diffusion processes from open domains satisfying the exterior sphere condition belong to the Geiss-Besov space $\mathbb{B}_p^{\frac{1}{2p}}$. In the one-dimensional case, the same result is proven using Zvonkin transformation for untruncated exit times if the diffusion is uniformly elliptic.

papers.title: Addressable transversal CCZ gates on almost good quantum LDPC codes and nearly optimal magic state protocols
papers.summary: Assuming uniform subfield product expansion, we construct quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes with distances $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$ and at least $N^{1-ε}$ individually addressable logical CCZ gates on pairwise disjoint triples of logical qubits, for every fixed $0<ε<1$. With all logical qubits outside these triples initialized to $|0\rangle$, any subset of the corresponding logical CCZ gates can be implemented with a transversal physical CCZ circuit. As applications, we obtain two nearly optimal magic state protocols: CCZ distillation with arbitrarily small overhead exponent $γ\rightarrow 0$ and error suppression of nearly linear order, and a magic state fountain that directly prepares $N^{1-ε}$ encoded CCZ magic states with nearly linear distance $Ω_ε(N/\log^2N)$. The construction uses balanced products of expanding graph covers. The assumption concerns Reed--Solomon codes on three subfields of characteristic two and pairwise coprime extension degrees, a local hypothesis studied in a companion manuscript. We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.

papers.title: When Normal-Only Updates Are Not Enough: Test-Time Adaptation in Reconstruction-Based Time-Series Anomaly Detection
papers.summary: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practical TTA failures exhibit two distinct responses to this intervention, with 63 of 180 settings recovering a clear detection gain while 90 still show no clear detection gain; and (3) the updates reduce their immediate reconstruction objective across the evaluated settings, yet these reductions do not consistently lead to better anomaly ranking. Both failure patterns persist across alternative practical adaptation variants and modest perturbations of the benchmark labels. Together, these findings show that improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution to reconstruction-based TSAD TTA.

papers.title: Physics-Guided Crystal Structure Elucidation from Powder X-Ray Diffraction with Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
papers.summary: Determining unique atomic coordinates from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) remains challenging because peak overlap, weak scattering from light elements, limited scattering contrast between elements with similar atomic numbers, and experimental noise render the inverse problem underdetermined. Here, we present XCAPE (XRD-Constrained Accelerated Prediction Engine), a crystal structure prediction (CSP) framework that integrates experimentally derived composition, unit cell parameters, space group, and PXRD data into a symmetry-aware evolutionary search. XCAPE explores Wyckoff-site configurations using tailored mutation operations, evaluates candidates by both energetic stability and diffraction agreement, and accelerates geometry optimization using a universal machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The framework recovered 71 of 77 database-derived benchmark structures (92.2%) from simulated PXRD patterns and all 12 reference structures from experimental PXRD patterns. It further identified 12 candidate structure assignments that are consistent with experimental PXRD patterns, lack matching entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), and are thermodynamically competitive at the MLIP level. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations showed that 10 of these 12 candidates lie within 10 meV/atom of the convex hull. By bridging experimental diffraction data and physically plausible atomistic models, XCAPE can provide structural insight into previously unresolved materials and support accelerated materials discovery in automated research workflows.
papers.comment: 15 pages, 7 figures. Supporting Information is available as an ancillary file

papers.title: Parity Push Post-Selection with Soft Parity Constraints for Quantum LDPC Codes
papers.summary: Post-selection lowers the logical error rate of a quantum error-correcting code by rejecting unreliable shots. For a code with $K$ logical observables, the logical gap, a standard post-selection criterion, involves $2^K$ logical classes, and existing approximations to it suffer from a non-convergence error floor or a shielding effect. We introduce a decoder-agnostic post-selection strategy for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, called parity push post-selection (PPPS), which re-decodes a shot once per logical observable with a push toward the opposite parity. Each push adds one check node and one variable node to the Tanner graph of the detector error model, and we accept a shot only when every re-decoding returns a solution in the original logical class. We show that, with degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding, PPPS accepts a shot exactly when the logical gap exceeds the push strength $λ$. Applied with the Relay-BP decoder to the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code at $p=10^{-3}$ and the [[144,12,12]] code at $p=3\times10^{-3}$ under circuit-level depolarizing noise, PPPS lowers the logical error rate by factors of about 50 and 75, respectively, at rejection rates near 1%. We observe that PPPS rejects failures that prior post-selection strategies cannot reject, and thus shows improved performance.
papers.comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables; Supplementary Information: 9 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables

papers.title: Charged Schrödinger blocks in $1+1$ dimensions from the quartic Casimir and endpoint equations
papers.summary: We construct charge-two Schrödinger conformal blocks in one spatial dimension, independently of any dynamical realization. We consider ordered vacuum four-point functions of fundamental fields of dimension $1/2$, with homogeneous Schrödinger equations at the earliest and latest insertions and interactions allowed in the intermediate two-particle interval. For reduced blocks analytic in signed spatial coordinates and even under simultaneous spatial inversion, two functions of the time cross-ratio determine the full spatial dependence: the collinear value and a rescaled mixed spatial derivative. An exact Kummer lift, built from confluent hypergeometric functions, gives this reconstruction. An operator identity reduces the quartic Casimir equation, modulo the endpoint equations, to an equivalent coupled system for this pair. At generic exchanged dimension, OPE conditions select a unique block up to normalization for each primary parity. We obtain collinear ${}_4F_3$ functions and sums of Kummer products, including the shadow branches. The blocks depend on the relative sign of the signed coordinates, distinguishing piecewise linear worldlines with an inflection from those with monotone segment velocities. In the Calogero model, we recover the previously derived bosonic four-point function and obtain its fermionic counterpart, with an independent integral check. At the diffusion-limited fixed point of $A+B\to\emptyset$, two blocks of opposite primary parity give the same collinear unlike-species response. Nonnegativity for all positions and ordered times selects the even family, thereby establishing that the response summed over species contains the even shadow pair with dimensions $Δ=1,2$. The nonnegativity argument demonstrates a concrete constraint for a Schrödinger bootstrap beyond collinear data.

papers.title: Hierarchical coupling in tripartite van der Waals cavity magnonics for a low-loss and tunable coupled-mode Hamiltonian
papers.summary: One of the greatest merits of cavity magnonics (CM) is the ability to explore rich coupled-mode physics, driven by the large \textit{in situ} flux tunability of magnonic resonances and magnon--photon coupling. Meanwhile, van der Waals (vdW) magnets offer an ultra-compact and highly integrated implementation of CM without complex fabrication processes. Nonetheless, the substantial magnon losses significantly hinder the combination of all these advantages. Here, we realize a hierarchical anti-crossing structure in a tripartite vdW CM with CrCl3 and realize an effective coupled-dual-mode Hamiltonian. We achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in loss while maintaining a strong coupling condition. Additionally, we theoretically confirm the feasibility of simultaneous and \textit{in situ} tuning of both loss and coupling by varying the magnetic field direction and strength. Featuring a micrometer-scale thickness and a width of a few millimeters, our device is significantly smaller than those based on bulk crystals or crystal arrays. Our results establish vdW cavity magnonics as versatile platform for investigating intriguing phenomena predicted in coupled-mode systems.

papers.title: GramStatTexNet: Efficient, Interpretable, and Neuro-Inspired Texture Analysis-by-Synthesis
papers.summary: Deep networks achieve high realism in texture synthesis but often rely on opaque, over-parameterized representations that have limited direct connection to biological vision. Neuroscience-informed pyramid models are interpretable, compact, and biologically inspired, but rely on small, hand-curated statistics sets that are difficult to generalize or extend. We introduce GramStatTexNet, a hybrid analysis-by-synthesis framework that combines the multi-scale Gabor filter structure of classical models with the flexibility of Gramian-based correlations, organized into structured filter families. This structured representation enables analyses that are challenging for deep-feature methods: each statistic carries a named filter-family identity, allowing us to decompose synthesis fidelity into per-family contributions and to learn an interpretable, low-dimensional embedding that preserves perceptual texture content. We compare our framework to classical and deep texture-synthesis baselines across diverse texture categories, and on multiple perceptual metrics, highlighting the compactness and interpretability advantages of this hybrid representation, alongside competitive synthesis quality. This same framework extends naturally to peripheral textures via spatial pooling, and to dynamic textures using a spatiotemporal filter bank. GramStatTexNet provides a unified, interpretable framework for analyzing and modeling visual information with natural extensions across space, time, and eccentricity. Project page: https://vdutell.github.io/gstn

papers.title: Interpreting Timestamp Permutations in Dynamic Link Prediction
papers.summary: Timestamp permutations are used to test whether dynamic link predictors exploit temporal information, but a performance gap can reflect changes in training, evaluation history, or both. We separate these effects with a crossed diagnostic and measure input exposure: whether altered histories actually change the predictor's inputs. On MOOC, TCL trained with binary cross-entropy gains approximately eight pairwise-accuracy points from original-chronology training under either evaluation history, while changing history at fixed weights gives only 0.03 points. The small history contrast reflects unchanged inputs for 68.37% of queries, stable rankings for most others, and cancellation of gains and losses. Under original evaluation history, suppressing explicit time encoding reduces the training contrast from 8.03 to 3.64 points, a paired reduction of 4.39 points (95% interval [3.68, 5.09]) across six seeds. DyGFormer shows corresponding training and history contrasts of 22.34 and 0.38 points across two seeds, despite greater exposure. Partial history permutations further separate nominal intervention strength, input changes, and aggregate accuracy. These comparisons turn a single permutation gap into interpretable statements about training conditions and model responses, while leaving the internal mechanisms of temporal learning open.
papers.comment: 5 pages total (ACM sigconf format). Companion code and trained models: https://github.com/karpovilia/tgn

papers.title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
papers.summary: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.
papers.comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Project page: https://middle-chunjie.github.io/AnyS1/

papers.title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.

papers.title: Modeling LLM Reasoning Dynamics with Structural Representations
papers.summary: Language-model reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations. We study how this temporal structure predicts continuation and the computation needed to analyze it. T/E/S combines text, local events, and spans of activity. Across reasoning and information-seeking tasks, events and spans improve next-outcome prediction in 70 of 76 evaluation groups for a Transformer and 74 of 76 for Qwen with LoRA. Span duration and preceding events are associated with transitions, and retaining event history across span boundaries improves prediction. We formulate budget-allocation counting and action-conditional continuation queries, prove counting hardness under explicit encodings, and derive conditions for affordable decision certification. In finite-process experiments, bounds that cancel shared continuation mass recover the same optimal actions as full dynamic programming while reducing mean inference CPU time by 77.7%. On 71 held-out HotpotQA and MuSiQue questions, a compact structural observer improves prediction of whether a fixed inference procedure finishes within a CPU allowance: Brier loss falls from 0.0836 to 0.0756. An annotation audit identifies substantial errors in that observer, separating this computational result from semantic validation of its features.

papers.title: Split-and-Learn: Decoupled Learning for Reactive Transport in Heterogeneous Marine Sediments
papers.summary: Reactive transport in heterogeneous marine sediments couples flow and multicomponent transport with nonlinear chemistry and evolving porosity and permeability, and its simulation over thousands of years is computationally expensive, especially when uncertain heterogeneity requires many simulations. We develop Split-and-Learn, a framework that keeps the sequential operator-splitting scheme of the full-order model and replaces each stage by a data-driven surrogate with its own structure. Transport is learned on a local data-driven multiscale space, either as a compressed reduced solution map (global inverse atoms) or as coarse-block pieces of the forward operator assembled into a Galerkin or least-squares Petrov-Galerkin system (local atoms). Chemistry is learned through bounded reaction extents with stoichiometric reconstruction, which preserves reaction invariants and nonnegativity. Flow uses learned interface traces and a reduced mixed multiscale solve that enforces coarse-block mass balance. We prove the stability of the split scheme with the evolving medium and bound the error of the learned solver by the accumulated one-step errors of its stages. Numerical experiments in two- and three-dimensional heterogeneous sediment domains show the accuracy and computational cost of the individual and combined learned stages against the full order split solver.

papers.title: A Comparison of Heuristic, Human-Sensitive, and Self-Play DRL Policies in Human-Agent Teaming
papers.summary: Dynamical Perceptual-Motor Primitives (DPMPs) offer a tractable framework for generating human-like movement dynamics in artificial agents (AAs) and have been used to support coordination in human-AI teaming tasks. Traditionally, DPMP controllers rely on heuristic (rule-based) decision policies derived from human behavior to guide goal selection and action sequencing. Although effective in structured tasks, such heuristics can be difficult to generalize to more complex settings, motivating interest in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches for learning decision policies for human-AI interaction. A key challenge, however, is ensuring that DRL policies remain aligned with human strategies, particularly when agents are trained through self-play. To examine this issue, we compared three target-selection policies governing DPMP-based AAs in a first-person herding task: (1) a human-derived heuristic policy, (2) a self-play DRL policy (SP-DRL), and (3) a human-sensitive DRL policy (HS-DRL) trained alongside a heuristic agent. Results showed that heuristic agents most closely matched typical human-human coordination patterns, followed by HS-DRL agents, whereas SP-DRL agents deviated most. These findings highlight the importance of human-informed training when developing DRL-based teammates and suggest that simple heuristic policies may remain an effective approach for designing human-aligned AAs capable of human-AI collaboration.
papers.comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Includes Supplementary Material A (1 page, 0 figures), B (1 page, 0 figures), and C (54 pages, 216 figures). Submitted to IEEE HMS for possible publication

papers.title: Strongly Suppressed Cosmic-Ray Diffusion in a Wind-Blown Cavity Environment of SNR G21.8-3.0
papers.summary: We report the discovery of a GeV $γ$-ray source spatially offset from SNR G21.8-3.0, while no significant high-energy emission is detected from the remnant itself. Using 16 yr of \emph{Fermi}-LAT observations together with $^{12}$CO ($J=1-0$) data, we show that the GeV emission is spatially associated with a localized molecular cloud located just outside a gas cavity whose boundary closely follows the SNR shell. This configuration supports a scenario in which cosmic rays (CRs) escaping from the remnant propagate through a progenitor-carved low-density cavity and illuminate nearby dense gas. Modeling of the cloud emission requires a diffusion coefficient suppressed by a factor of several tens relative to the canonical Galactic value, indicating strongly inhibited CR transport around the remnant. Rather than serving as a simple low-density escape channel, the wind-blown cavity appears to regulate CR propagation through local magnetic structure and enhanced turbulence. This system therefore provides evidence that circumstellar structures can control the escape and early transport of CRs around supernova remnants.

papers.title: Same Rank, Different Needs: Rethinking LoRA Redistribution in Federated Learning
papers.summary: Federated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables clients with different resource budgets to collaboratively fine-tune foundation models. To distribute an aggregated update within each client's rank budget, existing methods commonly retain its leading singular directions. However, directions that best reconstruct the update matrix need not best preserve its responses on a particular client's inputs: a lower-energy direction may matter more to that recipient. We formalize this mismatch and show that matrix-optimal truncation can incur arbitrarily larger response error than another readout of the same rank. Motivated by this result, we propose Receiver-Aware Subspace Adaptation (RASA), a plug-in framework for receiver-aware knowledge transfer. RASA uses compact diagonal input second moments to perform uncentered PCA of receiver-weighted update responses. The resulting readout is globally optimal for the rank-constrained receiver objective and preserves at least as much response energy as spectral truncation under the diagonal metric. RASA also introduces spectral-reference aggregation, which removes the personalized initialization offset while retaining the locally learned increment. Experiments on DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI demonstrate RASA's effectiveness across methods under resource, task, and data heterogeneity. In particular, RASA improves DomainNet-100 accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with FlexLoRA and achieves gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen SuperNI tasks and 4.37 on unseen tasks with modest overhead.

papers.title: Nonradial threshold scattering for the planar cubic--quintic NLS
papers.summary: We study the planar cubic--quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equation \[ i\partial_tu+Δu=-|u|^2u+|u|^4u, \qquad (t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2, \] with initial data $u_0\in H^1_x(\mathbb R^2)$. We prove scattering in both time directions when the mass of \(u_0\) equals the mass of the ground state for the focusing cubic equation. This resolves the nonradial threshold scattering problem posed by Murphy [\emph{Comm.\ Partial Differential Equations} \textbf{46} (2021), 2213--2234]. Together with the known subthreshold scattering theory and the existence of standing waves at every larger mass, this identifies the sharp mass range in which every $H^1$ solution scatters. The proof combines localized interaction Morawetz estimates with propagation estimates on moving halfspaces to control exterior kinetic energy.

papers.title: The Geometry of Mode Sampling in Reconfigurable MIMO Channel Extrapolation
papers.summary: Pattern-reconfigurable arrays acquire channels by distributing radiation modes across their antenna elements. Equal mode counts fix the observation budget while leaving a spatial sampling choice that directly affects reconstruction of unmeasured channels. We establish how this assignment enters the inverse problem through the receive aperture and the coupling between propagation paths. For an isolated path with calibrated positive real responses, the power-weighted variance of antenna positions completely characterizes the assignment dependence of the profiled angle information at fixed mode counts. We then construct layouts with identical weighted apertures and different path correlations, exposing a limitation of aperture-based design in multipath propagation. A paired simulation study evaluates balanced random, contiguous, interleaved, and equal-moment sampling using a common estimator with per-detection joint angle refinement. Balanced random sampling substantially reduces complete-channel error relative to ascending contiguous blocks when some modes are entirely unobserved, with improvements across nearly all tested scenes at high signal-to-noise ratio. When every mode is sampled, the mean benefit is more sensitive to rare large errors. Together, the analysis and experiments connect the spatial distribution of mode measurements to both extrapolation accuracy and reconstruction stability.
papers.comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, and 1 table. An 18-page supplement is included as an ancillary file

papers.title: Heights and energies of polarized fibrations of varieties
papers.summary: We study nef line bundles on polarized fibrations $(X/C,\bar{H})$, with a fixed nef metrized ample polarization satisfying $H^d=1$, where $d=\dim X$. We prove a quantitative arithmetic height inequality under relative metric positivity, allowing singular arithmetic models and relatively nef adelic bundles. The height deficit defines a local energy. For nef, relatively ample line bundles over finitely generated fields, this energy is bounded below for almost every complex or nonarchimedean local-field realization of fixed polarized global model data, outside one null set common to the entire relative metric class. The results include big non-semiample examples. For ample $L$ and smooth positively curved $\bar{H}$, the complex critical equation is the Calabi--Yau equation; at zero volume, projective bundles recover Donaldson's functional. We also study critical metrics and conjectural canonical heights defined by energy envelopes.

papers.title: Expressiveness and Convertibility of Rule-Based Access Control Policies
papers.summary: Rule-based access control models such as attribute-based access control support flexible policies based on rules with conditional expressions. The design choices in those models such as what is allowed in the conditional expressions or supporting deny rules may impact the range of the policies that are expressible. In this paper, we propose a systematic approach to investigate the semantics and compare the expressiveness of various rule-based access control models that can be built based on different design choices of rule structure and rule composition. Furthermore, we investigate the problem of convertibility of a policy from one rule-based model to another. This question is critical for policy migration to ensure that a given policy instance in a source model is expressible in a target model. Some of our major results in this paper include well-formedness properties for policy semantics, expressiveness hierarchy of models, and computational complexity of policy convertibility, all having important implications on the design and application of rule-based access control policy models.

papers.title: Kernel Design in Particle Mesh Ewald Methods: Splitting, Interpolation, and Upsampling
papers.summary: For more than thirty years, particle mesh Ewald (PME) methods have dominated the computation of electrostatic interactions in molecular dynamics. A PME method uses a splitting kernel to divide the interaction into a local part, summed within a cutoff, and a smooth part, computed on a grid with a spreading and interpolation (SI) kernel. The established methods use Ewald's Gaussian split with B-spline SI kernels, and the recent Ewald summation with prolates accelerates them severalfold by using a prolate spheroidal wave function (PSWF) for both kernels. Neither choice meets two needs of molecular dynamics: a smooth energy, which long simulations need in order to conserve it, and a low-order SI kernel that stays accurate on coarse grids and gains accuracy as the grid is refined. We present a framework for designing both kernels to meet these needs. For inverse powers from the Coulomb to the dispersion interaction, our splits make the local part smooth at the cutoff to any order while keeping the Fourier concentration of the smooth part close to optimal. We show that with analytic differentiation, the force error of a continuous SI kernel of fixed shape vanishes under grid refinement only if every particle, wherever it lies, gives the grid its exact charge and dipole moment. Our SI kernel for the Coulomb interaction ensures this by construction and is twice continuously differentiable. Compared with the B-spline of the same order, it needs fewer grid points by a factor of up to nearly five; on coarse grids, it mostly needs a lower order than the PSWF kernel. In simulations of liquid water over 100 million time steps, the new kernels reduce the energy drift of both the established and the PSWF kernels by about three orders of magnitude, with a smaller force error than either. Existing PME codes can adopt them by replacing only the two kernels and the Fourier multiplier.

papers.title: Gopakumar-Vafa invariants and Mordell-Weil lattices
papers.summary: Let $X\to B$ be a Weierstrass fibration with integral fibers from a smooth Calabi--Yau threefold to a del Pezzo surface. For a smooth curve $D\subset B$ with smooth inverse image $Y$, we decompose the moduli fiber of stable sheaves with Euler characteristic one and projected cycle $D$. In fiber degree $k$, its components are indexed by all sections $C$ of $Y\to D$ with $\tfrac12\langle C,C\rangle\leq k$, where $\langle\, ,\,\rangle$ is the Mordell--Weil height pairing. For infinitesimally rigid sections we compute the GV contributions, recovering the $E_8$ theta product over a $(-1)$-curve. We formulate the corresponding conjecture for families of sections.

papers.title: A Complete Classification of the One-Dimensional Nonlocal Eigenvalue Problem
papers.summary: We give a complete classification of the spectral stability of the following one-dimensional nonlocal eigenvalue problem (NLEP) $$ \partial_x^2φ-φ+pw^{p-1}φ-γ(p-1)\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}}w^{r-1}φdx}{\int_{\mathbb{R}}w^r dx}w^p=λφ, $$ where $w$ is the unique positive even solution of $w''-w+w^p=0$ decaying at infinity, $p,r>1$, and $γ\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\Reγ\ge0$. This type of NLEP appears frequently in pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems. We show that on the even subspace, strict spectral stability holds exactly for $\Reγ>1$ when $r=(p+3)/2$. In the $γ$-plane, when $r>(p+3)/2$, two conjugate boundary arcs open to the left from $γ=1$, and the strictly stable region lies to their right. When $r<(p+3)/2$, the arcs open to the right, and the strictly stable region lies between them. Their common endpoint is $γ=1$ when $r\ge(p-1)/2$ and $γ=γ_H>1$ when $1<r<(p-1)/2$. In each case, the two arcs approach a common vertical asymptote. As an application, for real $γ\ge0$, the condition for strict spectral stability is $γ>1$ when $r\ge(p-1)/2$ and $γ>γ_H$ when $1<r<(p-1)/2$, where $γ_H>1$ is the value at which a conjugate pair of eigenvalues crosses the imaginary axis. The key ingredient in determining how the number of eigenvalues in the open right half-plane changes at imaginary-axis crossings is a cumulative estimate for the mixed-sign spectral weights that arise for certain $p$ and $r$ with $1<p<3$ and $1<r<2$.

papers.title: Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models
papers.summary: Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.

papers.title: Circuit spectra for binary matroids
papers.summary: The circuit spectrum of a matroid is defined to be the set of circuit sizes. The circuit $e$-spectrum of a matroid is the set of circuit sizes of the matroid containing the element $e$. The circuit spectrum problem is an important problem. Erdős (1992) conjectured that every connected graph $G$ with girth $g$ and average degree $d$ has a cycle spectrum of size at least $Ω(d^{\lfloor (g-1)/2 \rfloor})$. Sudakov and Verstraëte (2008) proved the full conjecture of Erdős in a stronger form. It is natural to consider the size of the circuit spectra of binary matroids. Murty (1971) characterized all connected binary matroids with circuit spectra of size one. Lemos et al. (2011) characterized the connected binary matroids with circuit spectra of size two, where the largest size is odd. For general binary matroids, it is still an open question to find a lower bound for the size of the circuit spectra. In this paper, we give best-possible such lower bounds for connected binary matroids that do not contain both the Fano matroid and its dual as minors. Let $M$ be a simple connected binary matroid that does not have both the Fano matroid and its dual as a minor, and $d\geq 3$ be the minimum cocircuit size of $M$. We prove that (1) for each element $e$ of $M$, the circuit $e$-spectrum of $M$ must have size at least $d-2$. This bound is best possible. (2) The circuit spectrum of $M$ must have size at least $d-1$, unless $M\cong F_7,F_7^*,R_{10}$. In exceptional cases, the spectrum of $M$ has size equal to $d-2$.

papers.title: Toward Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Neural AC Power Flow
papers.summary: Growing uncertainty in power system operations from renewables integration, extreme weather, and data center loads challenges the reliability of traditional power flow solvers at scale. Machine learning-based proxies are a potentially promising alternative, but the prohibitive cost of generating training data for large grids makes out-of-distribution generalization a key capability for deployment; currently, models trained on small grids lack that capability. In this work, we systematically evaluate how physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and perturbation-based data augmentation improve the zero-shot transfer of three graph neural network-based power flow models from smaller systems to a larger, unseen 500-bus system. We find that (1) physics-informed losses improve transfer relative to purely supervised objectives; (2) multi-grid training on smaller systems matches the best single grid but does not close the gap to target-grid training; (3) perturbation-based augmentation on edge attributes improves transfer by up to 54.6%; and (4) random line/generator dropout does not consistently improve performance.
papers.comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Accepted as an oral presentation at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI Foundations for Power Grids: From Models to Deployment at Scale (AI4PowerGrids), Sydney, Australia

papers.title: AdaS-ViT: Test-Time Adaptive Routing for Spiking Vision Transformers with Ultra-High Energy Efficiency
papers.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise event-driven and energy-efficient vision, yet existing spiking vision transformers (S-ViTs) largely confine spiking tokens to fixed and uniform firing schemes along the temporal, spatial and channel dimensions, whereas suppressing the computational redundancy thus incurred calls for adaptive firing mechanisms that operate jointly across all three axes at test time. To this end, we propose the Adaptive Efficient Integrate-and-Fire (AdaE-IF) model, which consults the attention score of each spiking token and routes salient regions to fine-grained firing patterns while assigning energy-frugal coarse patterns to the remaining regions. Building on AdaE-IF, we further introduce Spiking Gated Self-Attention (S-GSA) and Spiking Local-Gated Unit (S-LGU), which enforce selective spike emission at token and channel granularity. We integrate the aforementioned mechanisms and modules into AdaS-ViT, a test-time adaptive-routing architecture trained with a progressive spatio-temporal curriculum that stabilizes the co-adaptation of firing precision and routing masks. Extensive experiments across benchmarks spanning diverse data scales and modalities demonstrate that AdaS-ViT consistently achieves highly competitive performance. Notably, on ImageNet-1k it consumes only 1.02 to 2.45 millijoules per image and attains an accuracy-per-energy ratio of 32$\times$ to 72$\times$, operating in an economical inference regime and thereby pushing the energy-efficiency boundary further.

papers.title: XANES-Guided Molecular Structure Generation via Conditional Diffusion and Forward Spectral Prediction
papers.summary: Reconstructing complete molecular structures from X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra remains challenging because the spectra primarily encode local chemical environments, with overlapping contributions from multiple absorbing sites. Here, we develop an inverse-forward framework combining XANES-conditioned diffusion-based molecular structure generation with forward spectral prediction for candidate selection. The inverse model generates atomic species, bond connectivity, and three-dimensional coordinates from C, N, and O K-edge XANES, given only the total atom count without molecular formulas or element-specific atom counts. Combining all three absorption edges substantially improves structural recovery, achieving a best-of-10 exact-match rate of 56.6% across 2,888 test molecules. The generated candidates also reproduce functional groups and structural motifs, achieving a macro-averaged F1 score of 0.951 across 21 categories. Ranking candidates by agreement between input and forward-predicted spectra increases the exact-match rate from 24.3% for unranked top-1 selection to 43.9%. This spectral-consistency criterion also enables atom count estimation, identifying the correct count for 65.6% of molecules among seven tested values. Application to experimental spectra yields an exact structural match for imidazole and recovers characteristic functional groups in two additional molecules, while revealing limitations due to simulation-experiment spectral discrepancies. These findings establish an inverse-forward approach for reconstructing whole-molecule structures from complementary element-specific XANES information.

papers.title: Towards Environment-Aware 6G Network Planning: An Any-to-Any Channel Knowledge Map Approach
papers.summary: Planning sixth-generation (6G) networks for reliable coverage across diverse environments is challenging, as it requires channel knowledge between candidate network node locations and potential service regions. This article proposes an environment-aware network planning framework based on any-to-any (X2X) channel knowledge maps (CKMs), which characterize channels between arbitrary transmitter-receiver location pairs. Within this framework, we first construct X2X CKMs from environmental information, sparse channel measurements, or both, with map types and spatial resolutions selected according to the planning task. We then use these maps to predict coverage and optimize network deployment and configuration subject to service requirements and practical constraints, while accounting for subsequent network operation. Finally, field measurements assess channel prediction accuracy and deployment performance, providing feedback for CKM correction and deployment refinement. We discuss implementation methods and tradeoffs across these stages. Case studies illustrate the effectiveness of the framework for indoor intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) deployment and outdoor base station (BS) deployment. Live-network trials further demonstrate coverage gains from IRS deployment and BS reconfiguration, with measurement feedback supporting CKM calibration and configuration refinement.

papers.title: When Price Charts Rhyme: Historical Visual Retrieval for Stock Return Prediction
papers.summary: We study whether visually similar price histories predict similar future returns, using a vision model to retrieve each stock's most similar charts from three decades of U.S. price histories. A representation pretrained only on natural images already retrieves neighbors whose realized returns predict the cross-section of stock returns. Aligning the representation with subsequent returns more than doubles the strategy's Sharpe ratio and outperforms a convolutional neural network trained directly on chart images. The predictability is concentrated among stocks with greater limits to arbitrage. Returns and order imbalances around portfolio formation indicate that the signal identifies temporary selling pressure that partially reverts. A sparse autoencoder traces the return-aligned signal to recurring visual states that determine which historical charts are retrieved. Our approach traces each forecast to dated historical charts, making it more transparent than direct image-to-return models and linking rule-based technical analysis with machine-learning chart reading.

papers.title: Optimal homological stability: bounding secondary terms of Cohen-Lenstra moments and $S_d$-fields over $\mathbb{F}_q[t]$
papers.summary: We prove an explicit stability line for the homology $H_i(\mathrm{Hur}_n^c,\mathbb{Q})$ of any Hurwitz space associated to a finite rack $c$ depending only on its homology up to some finite $n$. Moreover, as the range of $n$ increases, the slope of the resulting stability line converges to the optimal slope. Thus, for any Hurwitz space, a finite computation will yield near-optimal bounds on secondary terms for the corresponding arithmetic statistics problem. Our theorem also applies more generally to higher order stability, Frobenius weights, and braided vector spaces. As a special case of our theorem, we can deduce stability lines depending only on when $H_0(\mathrm{Hur}^c_n,\mathbb{Q})$ stabilizes, which are sharp in some cases. We apply this to two families of Hurwitz spaces to obtain bounds on the secondary term for (1) the number of $S_d$-degree $d$ function fields with squarefree discriminant, and (2) Cohen-Lenstra moments.

papers.title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
papers.summary: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.
papers.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Physical World AI: Geometry, Characteristics, and Multimodal Sensing

papers.title: HypoLoop: Revising Weight-Editing Plans from Scientific Feedback
papers.summary: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors. Effective updates depend on which parameters change and which errors drive the correction. We introduce HypoLoop, a family of native weight-editing methods that connects these choices to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided policies produce editing plans; numerical solvers compute weight patches, and internal validation selects the deployed predictor. Successive observations and validation records support revisions to editable locations and fitting rules. Experiments cover 22 scientific tasks and both DeepSeek and Claude. On Burgers, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On DIODE, positive-residual weighting reduces absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 13.35% in internal cross-validation, with the same 33 editable coordinates. Revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final AbsRel by 10.59% relative to keeping the initial plan fixed. SpaceNet7 and Make3D connect accepted edits to improved spatial predictions. These results show how experimental evidence can shape the update problem itself. Code: https://github.com/limengran98/HypoLoop.

papers.title: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
papers.summary: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $τ^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($τ^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $ρ$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.

papers.title: JITAtlas: Checking Lifetime and Protection Obligations in Compiler Rewrites
papers.summary: Compiler rewrites can preserve returned values while violating object lifetime or ownership. Such failures arise when a rewrite changes when an object remains live, whether a borrowed pointer stays supported, or what ownership reaches the caller. We present JITAtlas, a source-level checker that reconstructs reference and target computations from optimizer code and checks valid uses, continuous borrow support, and caller-visible ownership. On a 58-input benchmark constructed and labeled independently of JITAtlas output, JITAtlas detects all 29 defects and reports none of 29 safe inputs; PyRefcon detects 20 defects and CpyChecker 18. Across three CPython snapshots, JITAtlas extracts 3,332 rewrite alternatives, retains 801 under recovered receiving contexts, and reports 194 violations. Manual review confirms 92 reports, giving 47.42% precision. End-to-end analysis takes 35.56-42.31 s per snapshot. JITAtlas further identifies 15 new bugs across five failure classes, each with a reproducible proof of concept.

papers.title: Chirp-stabilized charging of a two-level quantum battery
papers.summary: Resonantly driven two-level quantum batteries (QBs) suffer from strong pulse-area dependence and energy backflow inherent to Rabi oscillations. To address this limitation, we propose charging of a two-level QB with chirped pulses. We investigate four charging protocols formed by pairing hyperbolic secant (sech) or Gaussian pulse envelopes with linear or hyperbolic-tangent (tanh) frequency sweeps. We show that sufficiently strong chirp modulation converts the charging mechanism from pulse-area-governed Rabi rotation to adiabatic rapid passage. We analyze the underlying adiabatic dynamics and derive the criteria for robust chirped charging, which incorporate the sweep bandwidth, nonadiabatic transitions, and dissipative effects. Under strong chirp modulation, the final stored energy and ergotropy converge to stable plateaus that are nearly insensitive to the pulse area across an extended parameter window. Of the four schemes, the sech pulse with tanh chirp delivers the widest ergotropy plateau and the weakest pulse area sensitivity. Compared with counterdiabatic driving, the sech tanh protocol attains stable charging performance without demanding an extra drive quadrature. Furthermore, this chirp-enabled charging is resilient to static detuning and weak-to-moderate dissipation. This work establishes a practical route toward robust charging of quantum batteries using chirped pulse control.

papers.title: Producing $μ$Bq/m3-level low-226Ra ultrapure water for the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory
papers.summary: The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), a 20 kton low-background liquid-scintillator (LS) detector, was designed primarily to determine the neutrino mass ordering. JUNO requires ultrapure water (UPW) with a Ra concentration < 50~$μ$Bq/m3 because of the direct liquid-liquid contact between LS and UPW during detector filling. To meet this stringent requirement, a high-sensitivity measurement system capable of detecting Ra in water down to 3.9 $μ$Bq/m3 was developed, and the 100 t/h UPW production process was optimized. By integrating selective ion-exchange resin with membrane-based separation technologies, the system consistently produced UPW with a Ra concentration of <4$μ$Bq/m3, exceeding the JUNO specification and, to our knowledge, representing one of the lowest reported levels achieved at this engineering scale. This paper describes the design and implementation of JUNO's UPW system and the high-sensitivity Ra measurement platform, together with a systematic evaluation of Ra removal efficiencies across the purification train and validation of the final water quality.

papers.title: Fisher Information Characterization in GNSS DPE under Multipath-Induced Channel Uncertainty
papers.summary: The availability and utilization of Fisher information in global navigation satellite system (GNSS) direct position estimation (DPE) under multipath-induced channel uncertainty are investigated. First, a unified estimation-theoretic framework is developed to characterize information mapping and utilization across direct and two-step receivers. Next, a scalar-equivalent statistical channel model for short-delay multipath is established via least-squares (LS) projection. Based on this model, receiver-state Cramér-Rao bounds (CRBs) are derived under perfect and statistical channel knowledge, while misspecified CRBs (MCRBs) are derived under a simplified deterministic complex-gain model that neglects channel uncertainty. The closed-form approximations and asymptotic analyses of the derived bounds further reveal how channel uncertainty affects different components of waveform-domain Fisher information. Our results reveal that: 1) DPE and fully coupled two-step estimation achieve comparable accuracy, whereas the performance loss caused by sequential decoupling substantially exceeds the additional loss from suboptimal weighting; 2) under statistical channel knowledge, improving received signal quality does not necessarily yield noticeable positioning gains; 3) positioning information remains available even as the coherent channel mean vanishes; and 4) neglecting channel randomness causes the MCRBs to diverge in this limit and can introduce positioning error floors that become more pronounced with longer observations.
papers.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

papers.title: Rational Ensemble Logic for Cohort Discovery with Real-World Electrophysiology Data
papers.summary: Biomedical knowledge representation should make the passage from observations to conclusions transparent, rigorous, understandable, explainable, and reproducible (TRUER). We introduce Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL) for specifying temporal phenotypes in real-world electrophysiology data (RWED), with a meaning independent of the implementation software. QEL combines three parameterized modal operators (exact displacement, bounded existence, and bounded universality) over rational time with Boolean connectives and first-order quantification. Its Labeled Interval Ensemble (LINE) semantics represents annotated records as finite interval ensembles. We relate the operators to morphological operations and develop endpoint-array algorithms and finite rational evidence sets for model checking. We prove closure and semantic correctness of the interval operations, obtain finite evidence sets by quantifier elimination, and establish polynomial data complexity for fixed formulas. On 54 manually constructed records, a prototype agreed with the assigned outcomes for base and strict post-ictal generalized EEG suppression (PGES) queries. A separate feasibility experiment over 1,976 patients identified 37 qualifying patients and 45 annotation patterns in 16 seconds. The released prototype uses endpoint candidates and numerical tolerances. QEL supports the TRUER principle through explicit phenotype definitions, precise semantics, and provably correct evaluation procedures, with rational witnesses for existential queries. These provide a logical foundation for formal specification and correctness of algorithms that are independent of specific clinical interpretation, data annotation quality, and software implementation.

papers.title: Functorial height and Orlov's rationality conjecture
papers.summary: An exceptional collection in the derived category of a smooth projective variety may fail to generate the whole category, and this failure cannot be detected by K-theory or by Hochschild homology. Kuznetsov's height detects it through Hochschild cohomology, that is, through natural transformations from the identity functor to its shifts. We replace the identity functor by an arbitrary endofunctor $F$ and define the height of a collection with coefficient $F$. It controls, in a range of degrees, the restriction of natural transformations $\mathrm{id}\to F$ to the orthogonal complement of the collection, and it is computed from the collection by a finite complex. For collections of line bundles on surfaces whose Hom divisors have nonnegative canonical degree, the tensor product with a skyscraper sheaf has height exactly two, and the projections of skyscraper sheaves form a two-dimensional family of point-like objects in the orthogonal complement. We apply these tools to Orlov's rationality conjecture. A smooth projective complex surface is rational if its derived category has a full exceptional collection in which all members except possibly one are line bundles, or one that consists of at most three completely orthogonal blocks of arbitrary objects; we also obtain rationality in several cases with four blocks or with a hereditary component. If $S\times\mathbb P^1$ has a full exceptional collection of the form $(M_i\boxtimes\mathcal O(a_i))$, then the $M_i$ with relative degrees of a fixed parity form a full exceptional collection on $S$; consequently $S$ is rational whenever $S\times\mathbb P^1$ has a full exceptional collection of line bundles. Finally, we show that the general case of the conjecture for surfaces is equivalent to the surjectivity and injectivity of two maps in Hochschild cohomology.

papers.title: Helicity-squared scaling of post-eikonal phases for electromagnetic and gravitational waves in Ricci-flat spacetimes
papers.summary: Spin-optical descriptions of electromagnetic and gravitational waves isolate finite-frequency corrections that are odd in the helicity. We study the complementary, helicity-even part of the first post-eikonal correction for scalar, electromagnetic, and linearized gravitational waves on Ricci-flat backgrounds. In a parallel-propagated null tetrad, the direct Weyl coupling of the gravitational field projects onto the circular transverse-traceless states as the multiple $2C_{\bar m m\bar m m}$ of the identity. The Ricci identity for the spin coefficient $μ$ then rewrites this projection as a total derivative plus optical terms. The helicity-even phase of a spin-$s$ wave, measured relative to the scalar wave, then obeys a helicity-squared law, $Δ_2=4Δ_1$, up to endpoint terms. The Weyl coupling is what completes the $h^2$ scaling in the gravitational case. For weak-deflection scattering by a Schwarzschild black hole we evaluate the relevant integrals along the ray and obtain $Δ_s=-3πs^2/(8Mωρ^3)$, with $ρ=b/M$. The same coefficient follows independently, and without reference to any frame or gauge, from the Regge--Wheeler phase shifts combined with the asymptotics of the rotation functions $d^l_{ss}$. Direct numerical integration of the radial equations confirms it. At first order in $M$ the helicity-even phase difference vanishes, as required by the Born amplitudes. The helicity-odd spin-optical sector and the helicity-even post-eikonal sector are therefore organized by the first and second powers of the helicity, respectively.

papers.title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII
papers.summary: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.
papers.comment: Accepted at the Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD) Workshop at ICML 2026

papers.title: Degree-three Euclidean spanning trees within a factor of 1.514 of the minimum
papers.summary: For every finite point set $X$ in a Euclidean space of arbitrary dimension, we prove that there is a spanning tree of maximum degree three and total length at most $(757/500)\MST(X)=1.514\MST(X)$, where $\MST(X)$ denotes the unrestricted minimum spanning-tree length. More strongly, for any root and any finite list of other points, there is a Hamiltonian path starting at the root whose length is at most $1.514$ times the sum of the root-to-point distances. The proof follows the rooted-path and variable-block framework used in earlier work, and applies Young's weighted-distance inequality to explicit rational mixtures of paths. Eight ordered radius regions cover the normalized domain. Their local estimates require only 29 vertex comparisons, all certified by rational arithmetic. The cover uses the three thresholds $1/4$, $3/8$, and $1/2$; its largest block has nine vertices. We give complete proofs of the normalization transfer, the global induction, and the terminal cases with zero or one actual tail point. We also give a fixed-dimensional cross-polytope lower bound, present Zbarsky's orthogonal simplex-cluster construction in explicit coordinates, and compare their finite-dimension bounds. The base cases complete the upper-bound argument before the lower-bound constructions are presented.

papers.title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
papers.summary: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.
papers.comment: Ongoing work. 67 pages with 34 figures and 37 tables. Project website: https://hackerchenzhuo.github.io/knowme-research-ai/en/ GitHub: https://github.com/hackerchenzhuo/knowme-research-ai

papers.title: Data Poisoning Attacks to Locally Differentially Private Triangle Counting Protocols
papers.summary: Local differential privacy (LDP) has become a crucial paradigm for privacy-preserving graph analytics, enabling graph analytics tasks such as subgraph counting without requiring a trusted curator. However, while LDP provides strong privacy guarantees, the integrity and robustness of LDP subgraph counting protocols in the presence of malicious participants remain poorly understood. In particular, since data are randomized locally before collection, it is inherently difficult to distinguish malicious users from honest ones based solely on their submitted reports, and small, protocol-compliant local manipulations can be systematically amplified through reconstruction and calibration into large global estimation bias. In this paper, we use LDP triangle counting as a representative task to characterize the vulnerability of LDP subgraph counting to data poisoning attacks.
